Hi Finn,

Do you recommend to implement this model in inlabru now? Can I fit the two likelihoods in inlabru even if they're not observed at the exact same locations?

Thanks

>
> This type of model structure can be implemented with the inlabru package, but as the package is currently undergoing a major overhaul to get rid of bugs etc, I wouldn’t recommend trying that at the moment.

> Finn
>
> > On 9 Jun 2020, at 15:05, Helpdesk <he...@r-inla.org> wrote:
> >
> > ﻿Hi,
> >
> > as simple as it might seems, I'm unable to see how can be done in a nice
> > way.
> >
> > there is a way out using an undocumented feature, 'same.as <http://same.as>', which allow
> > you to use 'alpha1' from another copy.
> >
> >
> > n <- 500
> > N <- 2*n
> > si<- sin(1:n /20)
> > si <- si-mean(si)
> > eta <- c(si+1, 10*(si+1))
> > s <- 0.1
> > y <- eta + rnorm(N, sd = s)
> > idx <- c(1:n, rep(NA, n))
> > idx2 <- c(rep(NA, n), 1:n)
> >
> > r <- inla(
> >    y ~ -1 + f(idx, model = "rw2", scale.model = TRUE) +
> >        f(idx2, copy = "idx", hyper = list(beta = list(fixed = FALSE)))
> > +
> >        f(intercept, model = "iid",
> >          hyper = list(prec = list(initial = 0, fixed = TRUE))) +
> >        ## same.as <http://same.as>='idx2' uses the same beta as 'idx2'...
> >        f(intercept.copy, copy = "intercept", same.as <http://same.as> = "idx2"),

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Copying a part of the linear predictor
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Copying a part of the linear predictor
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
the major overhaul is still ongoing, but there have been some updates on the devel branch on github that may be enough for this particular model to work.
inlabru.org <http://inlabru.org> has general examples on how to specify the models.
In your case you'll need to like() calls to setup the two predictor models, using a common set of model components,
beta0, x, alpha1, and other (but may be best to start with just those):

  components = -1 + beta0(map = 1) + alpha1(map = 1) + x(map = coordinates, model = some_spde_object)

The two formulas would then be
  formula1 =  y ~ beta0 + x
  formula2 = z ~ alpha1 * (beta0 + x)

With the current method in the devel branch, the effect should be that in the first iteration,
the first likelihood is used to estimate beta0, x, and the noise for y, and a noise variance for z (since it won't yet see the dependence on the other parameters, due to the starting point being zero.
In the second iteration, it should be able to use the previous estimate of beta0 + x to get an initial estimate of alpha1.
>From the third iteration, the second likelihood would start affecting the beta0 and x estimates as well.

How stable this is at the moment depends on your data. Let me know how it goes.
I expect a more robust optimiser to work soon, but for this model the above iteration behaviour would remain the same in the initial steps; it's the further steps that may a bit unstable now.

Finn

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Question about n for iid2d random effect
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Question about n for iid2d random effect
messages.body_plain:
Hi,  for model iid2d, then n=2*m, in you case, and ID would be 1:(2*m), when the data have the layout you describe.

The i th 2d component (u1,u2)_i, is found at location i  and i +m, in the iid2d model, for i =1…m.

If you want to check, you can always just simulate from the iid2d model and try to recover the parameters.

H

--
Håvard Rue
Helpdesk
he...@r-inla.org

> El jueves, 1 de octubre de 2020, 16:18:43 (UTC+2), Finn Lindgren escribió:
> > Hi,
> > the major overhaul is still ongoing, but there have been some updates on the devel branch on github that may be enough for this particular model to work.
> > inlabru.org <http://inlabru.org> has general examples on how to specify the models.
> > In your case you'll need to like() calls to setup the two predictor models, using a common set of model components,
> > beta0, x, alpha1, and other (but may be best to start with just those):
> >
> >   components = -1 + beta0(map = 1) + alpha1(map = 1) + x(map = coordinates, model = some_spde_object)
> >
> > The two formulas would then be
> >   formula1 =  y ~ beta0 + x
> >   formula2 = z ~ alpha1 * (beta0 + x)
> >
> > With the current method in the devel branch, the effect should be that in the first iteration,
> > the first likelihood is used to estimate beta0, x, and the noise for y, and a noise variance for z (since it won't yet see the dependence on the other parameters, due to the starting point being zero.
> > In the second iteration, it should be able to use the previous estimate of beta0 + x to get an initial estimate of alpha1.
> > From the third iteration, the second likelihood would start affecting the beta0 and x estimates as well.
> >
> > How stable this is at the moment depends on your data. Let me know how it goes.
> > I expect a more robust optimiser to work soon, but for this model the above iteration behaviour would remain the same in the initial steps; it's the further steps that may a bit unstable now.

Sorry, I clearly made a mistake, since alpha and beta here became random effects. Hang on a moment...

Finn

On Fri, 2 Oct 2020 at 13:24, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:

>

>
> Convergence, shown when calling this first:
> inlabru:::iinla.setOption("iinla.verbose", TRUE)
> fit <- ...
> iinla() iteration 1 [ max: 10 ]. Done.
> iinla() iteration 2 [ max: 10 ]. Done. Max deviation from previous: 3630% of SD [stop if: <1%]
> iinla() iteration 3 [ max: 10 ]. Done. Max deviation from previous: 583% of SD [stop if: <1%]
> iinla() iteration 4 [ max: 10 ]. Done. Max deviation from previous: 463% of SD [stop if: <1%]
> iinla() iteration 5 [ max: 10 ]. Done. Max deviation from previous: 137% of SD [stop if: <1%]
> iinla() iteration 6 [ max: 10 ]. Done. Max deviation from previous: 148% of SD [stop if: <1%]
> iinla() iteration 7 [ max: 10 ]. Done. Max deviation from previous: 45.6% of SD [stop if: <1%]
> iinla() iteration 8 [ max: 10 ]. Done. Max deviation from previous: 46% of SD [stop if: <1%]
> iinla() iteration 9 [ max: 10 ]. Done. Max deviation from previous: 24.4% of SD [stop if: <1%]
> iinla() iteration 10 [ max: 10 ]. Done. Max deviation from previous: 19.3% of SD [stop if: <1%]
>
> Partial INLA:::summary.inla(fit) output:
>
> Random effects:
>   Name  Model
>     beta0 IID model
>    alpha1 IID model
>    x SPDE2 model
>
> Model hyperparameters:
>                          mean       sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant    mode
> Precision for beta0  24753.56 2.61e+04   2485.991 17053.33   93269.68 6803.23
> Precision for alpha1     4.44 3.84e+00      0.527     3.40      14.59    1.51
> Range for x              5.98 1.45e+00      3.780     5.75       9.42    5.31
> Stdev for x              1.38 2.22e-01      0.994     1.36       1.86    1.32
>
> On Fri, 2 Oct 2020 at 11:19, Jorge Sicacha <jorges...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > I didn't have the devel, I installed it. I also updated INLA to the latest stable version, but now it get:
> >
> > "Error in inlabru:::component.character("beta0", map = 1) :
> >   argument "model" is missing, with no default"
> >
> > when I specify "beta0(map=1)"in the components and
> >
> > "Error: 'inla.sp_get_crs' is not an exported object from 'namespace:INLA'"
> >
> > when I specify  beta0 as just "beta0" in the formula.
> >
> > Find attached the code I used.
> >
> >
> > On Friday, October 2, 2020 at 9:33:37 AM UTC+2, Finn Lindgren wrote:
> > > And you’ve installed the current devel inlabru version from github?
> > > The CRAN version has a bug that prevents this from working, but I think the devel version should be ok.
> > > If not, can you send me the code so I can debug it?
> > >
> > > Finn
> > >
> > > > On 2 Oct 2020, at 08:04, Jorge Armando Sicachá Parada <jorges...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > ﻿
> > > > So far I'm doing it for simulated data. However, I'm stuck in this error:
> > > >
> > > > "Error in (function (data, model, stackmaker, n = 10, result = NULL, family,  :
> > > >   INLA returned message: Model component 'f(alpha1, ...)' have only NA values in 'alpha1'. In this case, either argument 'n' or 'values' must be spesified.""
> > > >
> > > > I have specified the components as suggested. I don't see where my mistake is.
> > > >
> > > > El jueves, 1 de octubre de 2020, 16:18:43 (UTC+2), Finn Lindgren escribió:
> > > > > Hi,
> > > > > the major overhaul is still ongoing, but there have been some updates on the devel branch on github that may be enough for this particular model to work.
> > > > > inlabru.org <http://inlabru.org> has general examples on how to specify the models.
> > > > > In your case you'll need to like() calls to setup the two predictor models, using a common set of model components,
> > > > > beta0, x, alpha1, and other (but may be best to start with just those):
> > > > >
> > > > >   components = -1 + beta0(map = 1) + alpha1(map = 1) + x(map = coordinates, model = some_spde_object)
> > > > >
> > > > > The two formulas would then be
> > > > >   formula1 =  y ~ beta0 + x
> > > > >   formula2 = z ~ alpha1 * (beta0 + x)
> > > > >
> > > > > With the current method in the devel branch, the effect should be that in the first iteration,
> > > > > the first likelihood is used to estimate beta0, x, and the noise for y, and a noise variance for z (since it won't yet see the dependence on the other parameters, due to the starting point being zero.
> > > > > In the second iteration, it should be able to use the previous estimate of beta0 + x to get an initial estimate of alpha1.
> > > > > From the third iteration, the second likelihood would start affecting the beta0 and x estimates as well.
> > > > >
> > > > > How stable this is at the moment depends on your data. Let me know how it goes.
> > > > > I expect a more robust optimiser to work soon, but for this model the above iteration behaviour would remain the same in the initial steps; it's the further steps that may a bit unstable now.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Finn

> > > > > > > Finn

> > > > > > > >    y ~ -1 + f(idx, model = "rw2", scale.model = TRUE) +

> > > > > > > > +
> > > > > > > >        f(intercept, model = "iid",
> > > > > > > >          hyper = list(prec = list(initial = 0, fixed = TRUE))) +
> > > > > > > >        ## same.as <http://same.as>='idx2' uses the same beta as 'idx2'...

> > > > > > > >    control.family = list(hyper = list(prec = list(initial = log(1/s^2),
> > > > > > > >                                                   fixed = TRUE))),

messages.body_plain:
Sorry if I am misunderstanding, but is it possible that your prior for the range is misspecified?  You have:

# Step 4 Define the SPDE.
spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh,
                            alpha = 1.5, ### give it some flexibility # https://groups.google.com/g/r-inla-discussion-group/c/ZhZVu8YPI8I/m/pUUWL1UZBAAJ
                            prior.range = c(100, 0.9), ### P(practic.range < 100) = 0.9
                            prior.sigma = c(5, 0.1),   ### P(sigma > 5) = 0.1
                            constr = FALSE)

I would have expected that if you want the range to be small you'd have ''prior.range = c(100, 0.05)". With ''prior.range = c(100, 0.9)", are you forcing it to be large?

> But one important question is this: why do you consider a long range to be a problem? The answer would depend on what you’re trying to accomplish with the model.

> If the covariates don’t capture all the large scale structure, but there is also uncaptured short range details, you may need two latent fields; one to capture large scale, and one to capture small scale.

> Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

so you just want to have a spatial model, beta, that is multiplied with known X-values for each observation?
Then you can supply x as a weight in th f() definition:
If you store the x-values corresponding to each observation in a column x, then the formula component is

formula <- y ~ ...  + f(betaindex, X, model="besag...", ...)

where betaindex is the index for the spatial region for each observation.

Finn

On Tue, 6 Oct 2020 at 17:55, Alex van de Minne <alexvan...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Dear all,
>
> I have a question relating the Besag models specifically. I wonder if I can have a parameter that is a function of its neighbors (following the Besag principles)? So instead of using the Besag model as an additive random effect, I want to more or less interact it with a parameter in the model.
>
> Say we have real estate transaction data. The properties themselves are denoted i, and the neighborhood is denoted p. y are transaction prices. Next I want to estimate a model as such;
>
> y_{ip} = \beta_{p} \times X_{ip} + \epsilon_{ip}
>
> where epsilon are the residuals that are normally distributed with mean zero and variance sigma. X could be square feet for example (let's keep it at one variable). Thus, beta can be interpreted as square foot prices, and the expected transaction price is the square foot times the square foot price (the latter we estimate in beta). Square foot prices (beta) are spatially related, and are thus assumed to follow a Besag model.
>
> Corresponding stan code (just the model block) could look something like this (haven't tested it, so I could be wrong);
>
> for(i in 1:N)
>  yVar[i]      ~ normal(  dot_product(beta[iD[i]]*SigmaBeta),X[i]), Sigma);
>  target       += -0.5*dot_self(beta[node1] - beta[node2]);
>  sum(beta)    ~ normal(0, 0.001 * Nn);
> }
>
>
> where ``iD'' gives the specific number of the neighborhood the property is in, node1 and node2 represent the neighboring properties (Nn is the amount of neighbors which is assumed to be always the same).
>
> Is there anything I can do in INLA to reproduce such a model?
> Many thanks,
> Alex
>
> (PS: in case you are interested I recently published a real estate article using INLA: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/1540-6229.12320 )
>

messages.body_plain:
The way I would think about models of this type is no different from any other model; just express the model in terms of how the latent variables are linked to each individual observation.
With j being the running index from 1 through N for _all_ the observations, regardless of which region they are in, the model can be written as

y_j = beta_{p_j} x_{j,p_j} + epsilon_j

where p is the vector telling us in which region observation j was collected.
This way of writing it allows the notation to be unaffected by such issue as whether there are the same number of observations  in each region, or indeed if some regions have _no_ observations.

But I may have misunderstood precisely what you meant by Y_{ip}.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Dear All.

I have this model implemente in stan, but I'd like to use INLA , if it is possible, to estimate.

A Coob-Douglas production function or similar in order to estimate the efficiency of several companies

y_i = f(x_i , β)exp( − u_i )exp(v_i )

My Stan model is like this:

model {
 alpha ~ normal(0, 100);   // intercept
 beta ~ normal(0, 100);    // slope
 sigma ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001);  // sigma is sigma
 lambda ~ exponential(-log(0.875));  // informative prior by literature for the hyperparameter of innefficiency
u ~ exponential(lambda);  // INNEFFICIENCY PARAMETER !!
y ~ normal(alpha + x * beta + u, sigma); //  "Regression"
 }

generated quantities {
 vector[N] eff;
 eff = exp(-u);  // computes de Efficiency for each company
}

Is there any way to use INLA in order to obtain this kind of models?

messages.body_plain:
Hi Josep,

if I read that Stan code correctly, you're really modelling log(y_i) there?
As in
  [log(y_i) | beta, u, sigma] ~ N( log(f(x_i , β)) - u_i, sigma^2)
where
  log(f(x_i,beta)) = beta_0 + x_i * beta_1
?
(but you have +u in the Stan code, not -u, so I'm not sure if it means what I think it means.)

The main difficulty would then just be that you have an exponentially distributed random effect u_i (in addition to the observation random effect v_i) for each observation?

We are currently experimenting with non-Gaussian effects in the inlabru package by treating them as transformed Gaussian variables, through copula transformation:
  u = qexp(pnorm(w), rate = ...)
where w ~ N(0,1).
inlabru linearises the expression with respect to w at the mode of the posterior, so you wouldn't get the full INLA approximation when using that approach, but it may be enough for what you need.

Finn

Dear Joseph,

Do you really need u_i to have an exponential distribution? The 97.5% quantile of u_i given the mean of your prior is qexp(0.975, -log(0.875)) = 27.6. Which implies that the Y_i with that u_i is a whopping 366 billion times larger than a Y_i with u_i = 1.

messages.subject_clean: using whole linear predictor of one variable as a part of linear predictor of other variable
messages.body_plain:
I have been utilizing the copy feature to use (multiples of) parts of linear predictor for one variable as a part of other variable (shared parts being either coefficients or spatial fields, as described in Virgilio's book).

Now, I am wondering if it is possible to use a (multiple of) complete linear predictor of one variable as a part of the linear predictor for other variable.

For instance, somthing like this:
X_i~Poi(m_i)
Y_i~Poi(M_i)

log(m_i)=eta_i=b_0+b_1*z_i+u_i
log(M_i)=a_0+a_1*w_i+a_2*eta_i

where u_i is a spatial random effect, z_i and w_i are fixed covariate values, b_0, b_1, a_0, a_1, a_2 are unknown coefficients.

All the Best
 Marek

you can. the construction is to use an iid model to equal the linear
predictor, then use the iid term further, and with copy to get it
scaled.

lin.pred=a + b*x

then define

	0 = -epsilon + a + b * x

here, 0, are the Gaussian observations with high fixed precision, and
epsilon is iid model with fixed low precision.

then

log(m) = epsilon

log(M) = 1 + w + copy.of.epsilon

so you need 3 likelihood models in this case.

as far as I recall, there should be an examples in the book of Virgilio
or the SPDE book.

H

messages.subject_clean: R 4.0.2 Update and Proj6 - altered mesh and predictions
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I've recently upgraded my program R from 4.0 to 4.0.2. I've also begun rerunning some SPDE models for publication edits that were submitted in late 2019. Many of the spatial projection commands in the code now result in warnings, specifically:

In proj4string(loc) : CRS object has comment, which is lost in output
2: In proj4string(loc.domain) :
  CRS object has comment, which is lost in output

I understand from a previous post mid-summer that most of these warnings are probably a non-issue. However, I've also noticed that despite running the same exact code over the same files, (e.g. changing nothing), the size of my mesh has changed slightly, and model output has changed as well. Even more of an issue are the drastic changes I see in the predictions that we generate from the final models. While they are identical to previous files in some areas, they are about half the value in others. The process I'm using to generate the predictions is developed from Fuglstad's (2017) suggested code, so I would expect some level of variation since we had to rerun the simulations. But, I would definitely not expect to see the level of variation that is being produced currently.

To further verify that there is in fact a difference between the versions and not the code, we've also rerun the models within an R 4.0 environment again. We get identical model output to that which we'd published in our manuscript, and predictions are much more on target with what we would expect from the model parameters.

If anyone has any suggestions as to what could be causing the difference and how to resolve the issue, I would really appreciate the input. The only thing I can think of was that INLA is acting differently somehow within the 4.0.2 environment and that it has something to do with the introduction of PROJ6. Even if that's the case though, I unfortunately don't know enough about the program to address the issue.

Thanks in advance,
KK

I noticed an earlier post from this past summer that discussed the implications of some of the warnings related to PROJ6.

To follow up on Finn’s comments, we also slightly tighten the step-size for numerical gradient/Hessian calculations from control.inla=list(h=0.01) to h=0.005, which in cases where the posterior is flat, might cause minor differences, but to the better. In these ‘flat’ cases I would suggests to rerun if you’re unsure, with

r=inla(…)
r= inla.rerun(r)

Other than the proj6 and related issues, there no changes which are due to the transition R-3.6 to R-4.0 which should cause your problem.  I guess you’re running the latest testing version, if not, please do.

H

--
Håvard Rue

he...@r-inla.org

> Hi,
>
> I've recently upgraded my program R from 4.0 to 4.0.2. I've also begun rerunning some SPDE models for publication edits that were submitted in late 2019. Many of the spatial projection commands in the code now result in warnings, specifically:
>
> In proj4string(loc) : CRS object has comment, which is lost in output
> 2: In proj4string(loc.domain) :
>   CRS object has comment, which is lost in output
>
> I understand from a previous post mid-summer that most of these warnings are probably a non-issue. However, I've also noticed that despite running the same exact code over the same files, (e.g. changing nothing), the size of my mesh has changed slightly, and model output has changed as well. Even more of an issue are the drastic changes I see in the predictions that we generate from the final models. While they are identical to previous files in some areas, they are about half the value in others. The process I'm using to generate the predictions is developed from Fuglstad's (2017) suggested code, so I would expect some level of variation since we had to rerun the simulations. But, I would definitely not expect to see the level of variation that is being produced currently.
>
> To further verify that there is in fact a difference between the versions and not the code, we've also rerun the models within an R 4.0 environment again. We get identical model output to that which we'd published in our manuscript, and predictions are much more on target with what we would expect from the model parameters.

messages.subject: mgcv baseline equivalent
messages.subject_clean: mgcv baseline equivalent
messages.body_plain:
The mgcv package makes it fairly easy to set up a thin plate regression spline, even in multiple dimensions for measurements on different scales (e.g., angles, speed, or time).

Consider the models: y ~ s(x1, x2) or even y ~ s(x1, x2, x3), with the x variables being vectors of different kinds of numeric measurements . The default "tp" basis tends to work quite well, but tensor / Kronecker options and others are of course available also.

Is there an INLA equivalent for a multi-dimensional smoother for data like this that tends to work well with some default settings? If a mesh is required, are there reasonably robust settings that can be specified relative to quantiles or some other aspect of the x vectors?  Most mesh examples I have seen involve spatial coordinates only and even if they apply to my situation I am struggling to see what good defaults would be.

For what it is worth, the one-dimensional spde smoother function provided by the BRINLA bri.adapt.prior works incredibly well and keeps much of the machinery under the hood; perhaps there is a generalizable multi-dimensional version of it? I am also aware of the rw2 / rw2d option, but it seems that may require a regularly-spaced lattice and I'm not sure that is desirable for this application (perhaps it is: others will know more than me).

I have also tried Simon's ginla function, which may also offer an avenue, but I am not quite sure if it is what I am looking for either.

Would appreciate any suggestions.  Many thanks.

Jonathan

messages.subject: Inla crash when fitting the CAR model for the shared components
messages.subject_clean: Inla crash when fitting the CAR model for the shared components
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am fitting a shared components model for three binary outcomes from a cross-sectional data. I have aggregated these outcomes to fit so as to fit this outcomes as shared components. I have the glm and glmm models and the models run nicely but inla crashes when fitting the CAR model on the data. Has anyone experienced such a problem? And if so, how can I solve it? Or is there a way I can these components model for a binary cross-sectional data? The below is the code I have used.

library("spdep")
library(INLAMSM)
library(car)
library(CARBayes)

BASEDIR<-"C:/Users/Moses Lwanda Ouma/Documents/Year2/Research Project/KENPHIA_MERGED/"
kenyacount<-readOGR("C:/Users/Moses Lwanda Ouma/Documents/Year2/Research Project/Kenya_Shape_file/Shapefiles",layer="County")

shared<-read_excel(paste0(BASEDIR, file = "Sharecomponents.xlsx"))

merged<-merge(kenyacount, shared, by="COUNTY")

##Compute adjacency matrix, as nb object 'adj' and sparse matrix 'W'
adj <- poly2nb(merged)
W <- as(nb2mat(adj, style = "B", zero.policy = T), "Matrix")
plot(merged)

names(merged@data)

nbkenya<-poly2nb(merged)

nb2INLA(file="merged.graph",nbkenya)

 # Compute expected cases
   HIV_PEVV <- sum(merged$positive) / sum(merged$obs_HIV)
 merged$HIV_EXXP <- HIV_PEVV * merged$obs_HIV

 # SMR
  merged$HIV_SIRR <- merged$positive / merged$HIV_EXXP

# Proportion of physical violence
  PHY_PREV <- sum(merged$expphy) /sum(merged$obs_phy)

  # Compute expected cases
merged$PHY_EXP <- PHY_PREV * merged$obs_phy
# SMR
merged$PHY_SIRR <- merged$expphy / merged$PHY_EXP

 # Proportion of sexual violence
SEX_PREV <- sum(merged$expsex) /sum(merged$obs_sex)

# Compute expected cases
merged$SEX_EXP <- SEX_PREV * merged$obs_sex
# SMR
merged$SEX_SIRR <- merged$expsex / merged$SEX_EXP

d<- data.frame(OBS = c(merged$positive, merged$expphy, merged$expsex),
                 PERIOD = c(rep("HIV_PEVV", 47), rep("PHY_PREV", 47), rep("SEX_PREV", 47)),
                 EXP = c(merged$HIV_EXXP, merged$PHY_EXP, merged$SEX_EXP))

write.csv(d,
  file = "C:/Users/Moses Lwanda Ouma/Documents/Year2/Research Project/KENPHIA_MERGED/d.csv", row.names = F)

# County-period index
d$idx <- 1:length(d$OBS)

##Number of variables (i.e., periods)
k<-3
# Define bivariate latent effect

model.indimcar1 <- inla.rgeneric.define(inla.rgeneric.MCAR.model,
                                        list(k=k, W=W))

##Prescribing constraints so that the random effects sum to zero
A <- kronecker(Diagonal(k, 1), Matrix(1, ncol = nrow(W), nrow = 1))
e = rep(0, k)

##The GLM model
IIM.GLM <- inla(OBS ~ 0 + PERIOD,
                 data = d,
                 E = EXP, family = "poisson", control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),inla.upgrade(testing=TRUE),
                 control.compute = list(dic = T, waic =T))
summary(IIM.GLM)

##The GLMM model
IIM.GLMM <- inla(OBS ~ 0 + PERIOD + f(idx, model ="iid"),
               data = d,
               E = EXP, family = "poisson", control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),inla.upgrade(testing=TRUE),
               control.compute = list(dic = T, waic =T))
summary(IIM.GLMM)

IIM.CAR <- inla(OBS ~ 0 + PERIOD + f(idx, model = model.indimcar1, extraconstr = list(A = as.matrix(A), e = e)),
                 data = d,
                 E = EXP, family = "poisson", control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),inla.upgrade(testing=TRUE),
                 control.compute = list(dic = T, waic =T), verbose = T)

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] mgcv baseline equivalent
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] mgcv baseline equivalent
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The rw2 model does not require a regular-spaced grid, since it implements the irregular location RW2 model from
  https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1467-9469.2008.00610.x
so that's the basic equivalent to the mgcv models.
There isn't a 1-1 mapping between mgcv models and inla models; both contain models the other doesn't, but there are some ways of getting equivalent models, and more ways to get similar models.

The TPS itself is a bit annoying, since while (in an additive Gaussian noise setting) the point minimiser of the penalty is the same as the point minimiser for the basic undampened (intrinsic stationary) 2D SPDE model, the induced Bayesian prior isn't the same.  However, you could use an inla.rgeneric construction to implement it (Note: David Miller and others have done something similar in the other direction so that you might be able to use a version of the 2D spde models with mgcv, as a smoothing penalty model).

To get 2D kronecker models, the "group" feature gives you a kronecker between an arbitrary inla model and another model (restricted to a subset of the models, but includes the rw2 model).

For 3D models, any available 2D model can be grouped with rw2.

For a model on continuous space, with data at irregular locations, you can use an SPDE model, with a triangulation mesh (the triangle nodes don't need to be located at the data points; the mesh just needs to be built to give a sufficiently fine spatial resolution for the function being modelled).

The interface doesn't have a direct kronecker model for 2D models, but you can build your own with the inla.generic technique that lets you define arbitrary models yourself.

I'm working on expanding the interface for spatial models so that user-define models can have an easier time combining models, by defining collections of 1D and 2D domains into a single mapping object, but there are other items above it on the todo-list.

But there is the inla.row.kron() function, that can be used to help:
If a basic model is u ~ N(0, Q^-1), and the observation level is linked to the latent vector u via a linear combination multiplication
  eta = A u
then a kronecker model v ~ N(0, (Q2 x Q1)^-1) has linear combinations of the form
  eta = (A2 rowx A1) v
where rowx is the rowwise kronecker product implemented by inla.row.kron().
Using this, you just need to figure out the 1D models first, and then use the above to combine them.

Finally, for Bayesian models, there is no universal way around setting the priors to reasonable values. There are attempts to produce "default priors", but they all rely on assumptions that are essentially equivalent to choosing priors in a specific way that is not applicable to all response variable models.
For example, the prior variance for a spatial field has very different interpretations in an additive Gaussian georeferenced model compared with in a log-Gaussian Cox process model, even though on the latent Gaussian level they look the same.
For intrinsic stationary models in inla, such as rw2, the scale.model=TRUE option can help you, by standardising the scale of the variance, but beyond that the user must have enough understanding of their own application to be able to choose reasonable parameters.

PS. My focus is now more on non-intrinsic models (i.e. with non-infinite range parameters like the rw2 and TPS), and non-separable models; except for space x time, separable kronecker models are mostly avoided in geostatistical problems.

Finn

> Consider the models: y ~ s(x1, x2) or even y ~ s(x1, x2, x3), with the x variables being vectors of different kinds of numeric measurements . The default "tp" basis tends to work quite well, but tensor / Kronecker options and others are of course available also.
>
> Is there an INLA equivalent for a multi-dimensional smoother for data like this that tends to work well with some default settings? If a mesh is required, are there reasonably robust settings that can be specified relative to quantiles or some other aspect of the x vectors?  Most mesh examples I have seen involve spatial coordinates only and even if they apply to my situation I am struggling to see what good defaults would be.
>
> For what it is worth, the one-dimensional spde smoother function provided by the BRINLA bri.adapt.prior works incredibly well and keeps much of the machinery under the hood; perhaps there is a generalizable multi-dimensional version of it? I am also aware of the rw2 / rw2d option, but it seems that may require a regularly-spaced lattice and I'm not sure that is desirable for this application (perhaps it is: others will know more than me).

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] mgcv baseline equivalent
messages.body_plain:
Finn:

Thanks very much for this thorough answer. This answers a lot of important questions. Variance/precision priors are actually a more intuitive way to control the wiggliness of the function for me, so I will take that option any time.

However, I struggle with choosing a sensible hyperprior for the precision on the rw2, even using scale.model=TRUE. I have read the papers discussing how one derives the pc.prior for the rw2 precision, but that still begs the question of what we would expect the variance to be in the first place. Certainly, one can fit the model in mgcv first (not a bad idea for quick and dirty exploratory work) and use gam.vcomp to get mgcv's interpretation of its spline structure in terms of a variance with intervals, but frankly that doesn't seem to work very well when I try to translate if over. Putting mgcv to one side (there is no need here to just replicate whatever it does), I've also tried to base the rw2 precision off the precision for the outcome variable , the precision that is fit by INLA when using the variable as an iid, and even the simple precision for the variable in the dataset to which I am applying the rw2 prior. They tend to give me fairly similar (bad) answers, with even the default prior being much better.

I understand that at the end of the day there is no substitute for knowing your problem and knowing your subject matter, but I would like to think I know both of those pretty well: it's the translation into a rw1 or rw2 structure that I am not finding intuitive, at least not yet. Is there any rule of thumb you or others like to use to get a sense of where the rw2 precision is likely to end up, perhaps a ratio to something else given the number of unique values or the ratio of the variance in the proposed rw2 predictor versus that of the outcome? I can certainly start with the default log gamma, move it up and down, and keep track of the WAIC conditional on the results being sensible. Maybe there just isn't an intuitive rule of thumb that works for most problems. That's ok: some problems are just tricky. But if there are any guidelines that anyone has found are useful in making educated guesses about a good rw2 precision / variance, I'd appreciate hearing about them.

Thanks again.

messages.subject: Temporal models within groups
messages.subject_clean: Temporal models within groups
messages.body_plain:
I have seen discussion of temporal models when the structure applies to the outcome variable as a whole, but often the relevance of the temporal effect is how members of a group change over that time period.

Consider 100 subjects measured over 20 consecutive time periods. If the performance of the subject is of primary interest, we care about how each subject’s performance changes over time, not so much how the population’s performance changes over time as a whole (although that may be worth accounting for as well if there is a true shared effect). We want to know not only who performs well or who performs poorly, but how they are trending over time and, if we forecasted, how they would be expected to perform in time periods 21 through 25 given the trend observed as they approached time period 20. Notably, periods 21 through 25 will not have been seen before so ideally the data structure needs to be willing to accept “new” levels of time period while still benefitting from the trend up through time period 20.

Consider this as a gaussian model with subject levels 1 through 100 and time periods 1 through 20.

This sort of temporal structure seems like a potentially unique area of strength for INLA. Some latent model options might include:

“iid” models, particularly for ease of modeling:
f(subject, model=”iid”) + f(time, model=”iid”)
f(time, subject, model=”iid”)
f(time, replicate=subject, model=”iid”) [
f(time, group=subject, model=”iid”)

some of the above instead using “ar1,” “rw1” or “rw2”, particularly if we want to effectively forecast on unseen time periods rather than just predict on some average of the past.

some sort of state-space model (like that from Virgilio’s helpful book <https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/inla-gitbook/ch-temporal.html#sec:spacestate>) incorporating a variant of the above.

Or perhaps the more intuitive approach here is to view the structures as f(subject, time) rather than the other way around. (Probably not, but it’s not always intuitive why a model structure is ordered the way that it is).

Can you shed some light on the best latent structure candidates for a model like this? Thank you.

Jonathan

messages.subject: Different estimated values of coefficients of LGCP w or w/o prediction data stack.
messages.subject_clean: Different estimated values of coefficients of LGCP w or w/o prediction data stack.
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA user.

I'm building LGCP model for about 20,000 points.

According to the SPDE-INLA book( Advanced Spatial Modeling with Stochastic Partial Differential Equations Using R and INLA), I built the LGCP model.

However, when I wanted to get prediction values for all of the study region, that is, when I stacked the "prediction" data using inla.stack, the estimated values of coefficients of the model were different from the model w/o "prediction" stack data.

What's weird, the more the number of prediction points is, the more different the estimated coefficients are (including the coefficients of predictors and hyperparameters for SPDE).
For example, with the built LGCP model, if I want to predict the point intensity with a resolution of 1km for the study region, the estimated absolute values of the coefficients of the model with "prediction" stack were estimated to be lesser than that of the model without a "prediction" stack. However, if the point intensities were estimated with a resolution of 10km, the estimated absolute values of coefficients of the model with a "prediction" stack were similar to that of the model without a "prediction" stack. Thus, the predicted intensities from the model of 1km resolution are overall lower than that from the model of 10km resolution.

I found a similar question in this discussion group. However, there was no solution to this situation.

Thank you in advance.

Best regards,
Jun-Sik Lim

messages.subject_clean: Including categorical variables with interactions
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm using a spatio-temporal spde model and would like to include fixed effects for a categorical variable (AMP, with four levels: Flinders, Freycinet, Beagle and Huon) and interactions with a continuous variable (year). I initially set this up by creating a model matrix and using expand.factor.strategy = 'model.matrix'. This worked, however I would like estimates for all levels of my factors and the interactions. Therefore, I switched to using expand.factor.strategy = 'inla'. messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Including categorical variables with interactions
messages.body_plain:
I’m not convinced anything is wrong, but if you want to keep all interaction you easily get some confounding issues, which makes, marginally, effects to be about the same, as only certain contrasts will be likelihood identifiable.  So you might have to define some linear combinations to extract what you want.

An alternative, is to switch to a sum-to-zero representation, like

> x = as.factor(letters[1:3])
> y = 1:3
> r = inla(y ~ 1 + f(x, model="iid", constr=TRUE, hyper=list(prec=list(initial=0,fixed=T))), data=data.frame(y,x))

So you get the overall mean in the intercept, and then the effects of ‘x’, 3 levels, which sums to zero.

--
Håvard Rue
Helpdesk
he...@r-inla.org

messages.subject: Spatiotemporal data: indexing question
messages.subject_clean: Spatiotemporal data: indexing question
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am modeling a moderate-sized dataset (3108*14) using a spatiotemporal hierarchical model.
Until now, I used the temporal index first then spatial index afterwards. After reading other threads in this board, I realized that the index 'should' be in spatial-temporal order. For example,
My data have had space-time indices as below (in case of spacedim=3, timelength=3)
space  time
1         1
1         2
1         3
2         1
2         2
2         3
3         1
3         2
3         3

But after referring to the answer for the other thread, the indices should have had:
space  time
1         1
2         1
3         1
1         2
2         2
3         2
1         3
2         3
3         3

Thus, my questions would be: 1) I am curious if my modeling was wrong for now. I wonder if the INLA algorithm automatically sort the results by its space-time indices by referring the column names defined in the f() function.
For your reference, my formula was

form.m42 <- Mortrate ~
  f(GEOID, model = "bym", graph = graph, constr = TRUE, hyper = hyp.prior) +
  f(year1, model = 'ar1', constr = TRUE) +
  f(GEOID1, UELAG1, model = "bym", graph = graph, constr = TRUE, hyper = hyp.prior) +
  f(year2, UELAG1, model = 'ar1', constr = TRUE) +
  f(GEOID2, UELAG1, model = "bym", graph = graph, group = year3, control.group = list(model = "rw1"),
    constr = TRUE, hyper = hyp.prior) +
  PELDER + PNONWHITE + MEDINCOME + PUNIVABOVE + PPOVTBELOW + PRURAL + PRENTER + PHSINGLE

In this case, 2) I want to know the INLA model using form.m42 will automatically sort the output by GEOID2 and year3 or others (e.g. GEOID1, year2, etc.).

Thank you.

Hi,
your results are probably ok; if you've been looking at the linear.predictor or fitted.values output, they will have been in the order that your index vectors were specified.
The only issue would be if you also looked at the individual random effect results separately, since they will have been stored in the second type of order (with space index varying fastest, and the time index varying slowly).

Finn

messages.subject: Specifying fixed effects priors for sites in survey data
messages.subject_clean: Specifying fixed effects priors for sites in survey data
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm running a binomial spde model for multiple species across multiple sites. I am interested in site level effects and interactions with a year effect (continuous variable). Some species have very low or zero presence at some sites and this seems to cause issues with estimates for site level effects and interactions and interpretation of these effects.

I note that the default prior for fixed effects is (0, 0.001). I have tried altering the precision and this has a profound (perhaps expected) effect on my estimates. I have included output below where I use a precision of 0.1,  0.01, 0.001 and 0.0001. I have used expand.factor.strategy = 'inla' in order to get estimates for all sites.

If I run the model as a glm without any latent effects I note that I have very large standard errors for sites and interactions where this example species is absent (Beagle and Huon) - see last output. This is a different model specification with treatment contrats, but I think the principle holds true. So, it seems that I require a large variance in those cases, and smaller when the species is present.

Is there a prior that would better suit than the default here? When I run the model for a different species the sites with high/zero abundance will change so I'd rather have something that could be used for all species.

TIA

Nick

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have not used R Studio server, the install system assumes you run on the system you’re on. So if you’re on a Mac, it will assume you want to run there. If you then ‘export’ your library to another OS, then it will use that os. You can do this manually, by downloading from

https://inla.r-inla-download.org/Linux-builds/

And simply replace the 64bit directory you want with the one you download from here.

I guess you’re on R-4.0 both places?

--
Håvard Rue
Helpdesk

messages.subject: Proper way to use inla.make.lincombs() for guassian models
messages.subject_clean: Proper way to use inla.make.lincombs() for guassian models
messages.body_plain:
Dear list:

I am trying to run a varying coefficient linear regression model and attempting to combining the fixed and random effects for both the intercept and the slope by using inla.make.lincombs() function. My code using a simulated data follows:

N = 100
x = rnorm(N, mean = 3, sd = 2)
y = rnorm(N, mean = x, sd = 1)
data.test = list(x = x, y = y, N=N, ID = seq(1:N), ID2 = seq(1:N))

fm.test <- y ~ x + f(ID, model = "iid")  + f(ID2, x, model = "iid")

lcs1 <- inla.make.lincombs (id = diag(N), "(Intercept)" = rep (1, N))
lcs2 <- inla.make.lincombs (id = diag(N), x = rep(1, N))
names(lcs2) <- paste(names(lcs1), "x", sep = "")

lcs.all <- c(lcs1, lcs2)

test.inla<- inla(fm.test, family = "gaussian", data = data.test, lincomb = lcs.all, control.compute = list(dic = TRUE), control.fixed = list(mean = 0, prec = 0.001))

After running, I got this error message:

Error in inla.inlaprogram.has.crashed() :
  The inla-program exited with an error. Unless you interupted it yourself, please rerun with verbose=TRUE and check the output carefully.
  If this does not help, please contact the developers at <he...@r-inla.org>.

And adding verbose = TRUE produces a lot of outputs, but I think the last few lines that reported the error probably is relevant:

section=[9] name=[lincomb.lc001] type=[LINCOMB]
	inla_parse_lincomb...
		secname = [lincomb.lc001]
		filename [C:/Users/danli/AppData/Local/Temp/RtmpmKYuPo/file66bc36b942f5/data.files/file66bc17804de6]
		file.offset [0]
		precision [1e+009]
		Open file [C:/Users/danli/AppData/Local/Temp/RtmpmKYuPo/file66bc36b942f5/data.files/file66bc17804de6] at location [0]
		Number of sections [2]
			Section [0] is named [id]

*** ERROR *** 	Section no [0] named [id] in file [68838736] offset[               0] is unknown.

I am positive that the way I specify the inla.make.lincombs() is not right (I copied it from the book "Spatial and Spatio-temporal Bayesian Modles with R-INLA," but that's for the "poisson" family model that has a legitimate offset, mine is a "gaussian" family model and no offset is needed), but I cannot seem to be able to figure it out the right way on my own.

Any pointers will be greatly appreciated.

Best,
Danlin Yu

messages.body_plain:
Hi and thanks for your email. The names used are case-sensitive, hence
'id' does not correspond to 'ID', which I guess you want, doing

fm.test <- y ~ x + f(ID, model = "iid")  + f(ID2, x, model = "iid")

lcs1 <- inla.make.lincombs (ID = diag(N), "(Intercept)" = rep (1, N))
lcs2 <- inla.make.lincombs (ID = diag(N), x = rep(1, N))

then its fine.

Best
H
